 ASHEVILLE, N.C. (WLOS) — Some states are trying to off-set affordability challenges by raising the minimum wage.
 "I think other states are recognizing, 'Oh, there's a chance for us to be a more desirable place to work, to live,'" said Sam Stites, the living wage program coordinator with nonprofit Just Economics of Western North Carolina.
 According to E conomic Policy Institute’s Minimum Wage Tracker , 16 states are planning to increase their minimum wage next year.
 "I do think just having that standard out there helps to raise wages across the board," said State Representative Eric Ager.
 However, North Carolina is not one of those states.
 DESPITE IMPROVEMENTS, SOME ECONOMIC CHALLENGES REMAIN 2 YEARS AFTER HELENE 
 "It’s a real failure of the general assembly, I think" said Ager.
 While the state isn't getting a higher minimum wage, there have been efforts to raise it. State Representative Eric Ager says he worked on a couple bills to raise it. But Ager says both bills died in the rules committee.
 "Both would set at least a $15 minimum wage eventually and then set a course for raising that by the consumer price index so that wage level doesn’t just stagnate over time," said Ager.
 Just Economics of Western North Carolina is also advocating for people to earn a living wage.
 "We want to see market wages and the minimum wage and the living wage eventually be the same thing. People should be able to work a full-time job and afford to live," said Stites.
 Stites says the living wage, or the minimum amount someone needs to afford basic necessities without financial assistance, is $24.10 an hour in Buncombe County.
 TRUMP ADMINISTRATION TOUTS $330M SOLAR INVESTMENT IN SOUTH CAROLINA 
 Jack Igelman, an Economics Instructor at Warren Wilson College, says while raising the minimum wage a significant amount may have more pros than cons, there’s always a trade-off.
 He says that while some people might make a higher wage, employers would have to make a set of decisions like whether to transfer the increase in wages to the cost of the product, whether to kick back hours for employees or to cut jobs.
 As for Asheville resident Patrick McNabb, he says he’s surprised that the federal government hasn’t increased its minimum wage from $7.25 an hour since 2009.
 "The rich get richer, the people on the bottom get less. It’s not fair," said McNabb.
